ProGRank: Probe-Gradient Reranking to Defend Dense-Retriever RAG from Corpus Poisoning

Xiangyu Yin Affiliation: Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden E-mail {yinxi,chengch}@chalmers.se    Yi Qi Affiliation: University of Leeds, United Kingdom E-mail Y.Qi@leeds.ac.uk    Chih-Hong Cheng Affiliation: Chalmers University of Technology, Sweden E-mail {yinxi,chengch}@chalmers.se Affiliation: Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg, Germany E-mail chih-hong.cheng@uni-oldenburg.de
Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the reliability of large language model applications by grounding generation in retrieved evidence, but it also introduces a new attack surface: corpus poisoning. In this setting, an adversary injects or edits passages so that they are ranked into the Top-KK results for target queries and then affect downstream generation. Existing defences against corpus poisoning often rely on content filtering, auxiliary models, or generator-side reasoning, which can make deployment more difficult. We propose ProGRank, a post hoc, training-free retriever-side defence for dense-retriever RAG. ProGRank stress-tests each query–passage pair under mild randomized perturbations and extracts probe gradients from a small fixed parameter subset of the retriever. From these signals, it derives two instability signals, representational consistency and dispersion risk, and combines them with a score gate in a reranking step. ProGRank preserves the original passage content, requires no retraining, and also supports a surrogate-based variant when the deployed retriever is unavailable. Extensive experiments across three datasets, three dense retriever backbones, representative corpus poisoning attacks, and both retrieval-stage and end-to-end settings show that ProGRank provides stronger defence performance and a favorable robustness–utility trade-off. It also remains competitive under adaptive evasive attacks.

Keywords:
Retrieval Augmented Generation Corpus Poisoning Robust Reranking

1 Introduction

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the reliability of large language model (LLM) applications by grounding generation in externally retrieved evidence [9, 10, 13, 16]. In practical deployments, the retrieval corpus is often assembled from web-scale or user-contributed sources rather than a fully curated collection, making the corpus an additional trust boundary for the RAG pipeline [5, 29, 30]. Modern RAG systems commonly rely on neural dense retrievers that rank passages by embedding similarity and pass the Top-K\mathrm{K} passages to the generator [14, 16, 23].

Among the emerging risks, corpus poisoning is particularly concerning. In this setting, an adversary injects or edits a small number of passages so that they are ranked into the Top-KK results for target queries and subsequently steer generation through poisoned evidence [28, 38, 40]. This threat model covers representative attack families, including retrieval-optimized poisoning [38], joint optimization with retrieval and generation objectives [40, 28], trigger-based poisoning that activates under specific queries [2], and misleading-evidence attacks that induce unfaithful or harmful generations [4, 26]. Our goal is to reduce poisoned Top-K\mathrm{K} exposure at retrieval time, thereby lowering downstream attack success, without modifying the generator or retraining the retriever.

Existing defences can be grouped by the stage at which they intervene. Generation-time defences change how retrieved evidence is consumed during decoding, for example via aggregation schemes [31], attention constraints [6], or activation-based analysis [25]. System-level approaches aim to identify and remove poisoned sources in the corpus, which often requires corpus-wide access and offline processing [36]. Retriever-side defences instead act on the ranking itself by reducing the chance that poisoned passages enter the Top-K\mathrm{K} set. However, existing poisoning-mitigation methods at or around retrieval often rely on auxiliary detectors or content-based filtering [7, 17, 34], dedicated reranking procedures [37], or hybrid pipelines that invoke language-model reasoning beyond retrieval [39], which can complicate deployment.

We propose ProGRank, a post hoc, training-free retriever-side defence for neural dense retrievers in RAG. As illustrated in Fig. 1, ProGRank performs a lightweight stress test on each query–passage pair by computing probe gradients of the retriever similarity score with respect to a small fixed parameter subset, namely a LayerNorm module at layer LL, under mild randomized perturbations of the retriever computation. From these probe gradients, we derive two complementary instability signals, representational consistency (Rep) and dispersion risk (DR), also denoted as the consistency penalty and the saturated risk penalty. Unlike generic uncertainty-based reranking, ProGRank probes parameter-space sensitivity rather than only representation-space variability, and combines these signals with a score gate that focuses correction on the high-score region that determines Top-K\mathrm{K} membership. The key intuition is that optimization-driven poisons can concentrate retrievability on a small set of perturbation-sensitive matching signals, which makes them more likely to yield unstable gradient responses under stochastic perturbations than benign passages. We do not assume that all poisoned passages are intrinsically unstable, rather, we treat such instability as a useful reranking signal for poisoning mitigation. ProGRank can be used in a white-box setting with direct access to the retriever, and it also admits a surrogate-based variant for settings where the deployed retriever is unavailable.

We evaluate ProGRank across multiple datasets and dense retriever backbones [1, 14, 16, 19, 33], under representative poisoning strategies [2, 4, 28, 38, 40]. Overall, ProGRank reduces poisoned Top-K\mathrm{K} exposure while maintaining retrieval utility, and lowers downstream attack success.

Contributions.

Our contributions are three-fold: (1) We propose ProGRank, a post hoc, training-free retriever-side defence that reranks candidates using probe-gradient instability under randomized perturbations. (2) We introduce a score-gated penalty fusion mechanism that focuses robustness correction on the decision-critical high-score region. (3) We show across multiple datasets, retrievers, and poisoning attacks that ProGRank reduces poisoned Top-K\mathrm{K} exposure and improves downstream robustness, while remaining effective under the adaptive attack settings considered in this work.

2 Related Work

Corpus Poisoning Attacks.

Corpus poisoning attacks inject or modify a small number of passages so that targeted queries retrieve them and downstream generation is steered [38, 40, 28]. Existing work studies direct passage injection against dense retrievers [38], end-to-end poisoning objectives for RAG [40, 28], trigger-style poisoning [2], and retrieval corruption through low-level perturbations [4, 26]; benchmarks further show that adaptive poisoning can degrade many defences [35].

Defences Against Corpus Poisoning.

Existing defences span multiple stages of the RAG pipeline [23, 29, 35]. Generation-time defences reduce the influence of retrieved evidence during decoding [31, 6, 25], system-level approaches trace attacks back to poisoned texts for cleanup [36], and retriever-side or retrieval-stage defences aim to prevent poisoned passages from entering the Top-KK set, often via filtering or detector-style scoring [3, 7, 17, 34], dedicated reranking [37], retrieval-stage content manipulation such as partitioning or masking [21], or hybrid verification with additional language-model reasoning [39, 29, 35].

Positioning.

ProGRank is a post hoc, training-free retriever-side defence that uses only retriever-derived signals, without auxiliary language-model inference, content filtering, or generator-side verification. Unlike filtering or hybrid verification methods [3, 17, 34, 39], it operates directly on query–passage signals from the retriever. Unlike approaches that alter retrieved content [21, 17, 3], it preserves the original passage content and adjusts scores in a post hoc reranking step. Unlike dedicated reranking procedures [37], it does not introduce a separate learned reranker or auxiliary model. ProGRank also admits a surrogate-based variant for settings where the deployed retriever is unavailable.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Setup

Given a user query qq, we consider a neural dense retriever with parameters θ\theta that ranks passage candidates p∈𝒟⁡(q)p\in\mathcal{D}(q) using the base score

sθ​(q,p)=⟨norm⁡(fθ​(q)),norm⁡(gθ​(p))⟩,s_{\theta}(q,p)=\left\langle\mathrm{norm}(f_{\theta}(q)),\;\mathrm{norm}(g_{\theta}(p))\right\rangle, (1)

where fθ​(⋅)f_{\theta}(\cdot) and gθ​(⋅)g_{\theta}(\cdot) are the query and passage encoders, respectively, norm⁡(⋅)\mathrm{norm}(\cdot) denotes ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization, and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle denotes the dot product. In the white-box setting, θ\theta denotes the deployed retriever. In the surrogate-based variant, θ\theta denotes a surrogate retriever used to instantiate the defence score when the deployed retriever is unavailable.

Let 𝒟clean\mathcal{D}_{\text{clean}} denote the clean candidate pool. An adversary constructs poisoned passages 𝒟poison\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}} either by corrupting clean passages or by directly inserting new ones, resulting in

𝒟=𝒟clean∪𝒟poison.\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{clean}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}.

Our goal is to derive a defended score s~θ​(q,p)\tilde{s}_{\theta}(q,p) built upon sθ​(q,p)s_{\theta}(q,p) that suppresses poisoned passages during retrieval. We formulate this objective as minimizing the overlap between the Top-KK set under the defended score and the poisoned set:

|TopKp∈𝒟⁡s~θ​(q,p)∩𝒟poison|,\left|\operatorname{TopK}_{p\in\mathcal{D}}\tilde{s}_{\theta}(q,p)\ \cap\ \mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}\right|, (2)

where TopKp∈𝒟⁡s~θ​(q,p)\operatorname{TopK}_{p\in\mathcal{D}}\tilde{s}_{\theta}(q,p) returns the set of KK passages with the highest defended scores.

We emphasize that this objective is a retrieval-stage target rather than a complete end-to-end safety objective. Accordingly, we evaluate retrieval-stage poisoning exposure separately from downstream robustness and clean-task utility in Sec. 4.1.

3.2 Stress Test-Based Reranking via Randomized Probing

Traditional neural dense retrievers rank candidates using a similarity score alone. This creates an attack surface for corpus poisoning: an adversary can craft or modify passages so that they achieve high similarity with a target query and enter the Top-KK results [38, 40]. ProGRank targets a practically important subset of such attacks, namely optimization-driven poisons whose retrievability is concentrated on perturbation-sensitive matching signals. Our key hypothesis is not that all poisoned passages are intrinsically unstable, but that this instability provides a useful reranking signal across diverse poisoning settings.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, ProGRank stress-tests each query–passage pair under mild randomized perturbations, extracts gradient-based instability signals, and uses them to adjust retrieval scores in a post hoc reranking step. For each query–passage pair (q,p)(q,p), in addition to the base score in Eq. (1), we apply a stochastic perturbation operator 𝒯⁡(⋅)\mathcal{T}(\cdot) for RR runs to obtain perturbed variants pr=𝒯r​(p)p_{r}=\mathcal{T}_{r}(p) for r∈{1,…,R}r\in\{1,\dots,R\}. In our implementation, 𝒯r​(⋅)\mathcal{T}_{r}(\cdot) can be token dropout, encoder dropout, or their mixture. Token dropout randomly masks a proportion of passage tokens, while encoder dropout uses the model’s internal dropout. Unless specified otherwise, encoder dropout affects the forward computation for both the query and the passage, whereas token dropout is applied only to the passage. For simplicity, 𝒯r\mathcal{T}_{r} denotes the stochastic perturbation used in the rr-th run without changing the notation for qq.

We keep the retriever parameters fixed and probe a small fixed parameter subset ϑ⊆θ\vartheta\subseteq\theta, instantiated in our experiments as a LayerNorm module at layer LL. Given a perturbed passage prp_{r}, we define the probe gradient as

gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=∇ϑsθ​(q,pr).g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\nabla_{\vartheta}\,s_{\theta}(q,p_{r}). (3)

We treat {gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)}r=1R\{g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\}_{r=1}^{R} as a sensitivity signature that captures how the query–passage similarity responds to randomized perturbations. From these probe gradients, we derive two complementary statistics: representational consistency, which measures directional agreement across perturbations, and dispersion risk, which captures lower-tail instability.

As directly computing gradients with respect to all retriever parameters is computationally prohibitive for ranking, we probe only the small subset ϑ\vartheta to obtain a lightweight sensitivity signature, following prior work that uses parameter subsets for scalable gradient-based influence analysis [22]. This view is also related to Fisher-score style representations, which characterize an input by its parameter gradients [15].

Representational Consistency

We quantify directional agreement of probe gradients across perturbations via a normalized gradient signal-to-noise ratio:

RepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=‖1R​∑r=1Rgr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)‖21R​∑r=1R‖gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)‖22+ε∈[0,1],\mathrm{Rep}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\frac{\left\|\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\right\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\|g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\|_{2}^{2}}+\varepsilon}\in[0,1], (4)

where ε>0\varepsilon>0 stabilizes the denominator. Larger RepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)\mathrm{Rep}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) indicates stronger directional agreement across perturbations. We convert representational consistency into an additive penalty:

PrepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=−log⁡(RepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)+ε),P_{\mathrm{rep}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=-\log\!\big(\mathrm{Rep}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+\varepsilon\big), (5)

so that candidates with low consistency receive larger penalties.

Dispersion Risk

Representational consistency captures directional alignment but does not directly quantify deviations from the mean gradient. We therefore define a relative deviation statistic:

devr,R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=‖gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)−g¯R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)‖2‖g¯R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)‖2+ε,g¯R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=1R​∑r=1Rgr,θ,ϑ​(q,p),\mathrm{dev}_{r,R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\frac{\|g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)-\bar{g}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\|_{2}}{\|\bar{g}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\|_{2}+\varepsilon},\qquad\bar{g}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p), (6)

and map it to a per-run stability score using an exponential kernel:

cr,R,θ,ϑ(q,p)=exp(−α⋅devr,R,θ,ϑ(q,p)),c_{r,R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\exp(-\alpha\cdot\mathrm{dev}_{r,R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)), (7)

where α>0\alpha>0 controls the decay rate. This yields a bounded score in (0,1](0,1] that decreases monotonically as the deviation grows.

To emphasize lower-tail instability, we aggregate {cr,R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)}r=1R\{c_{r,R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\}_{r=1}^{R} using a lower quantile:

cR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=Quantileτ⁡({cr,R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)}r=1R),τ∈(0,1).c_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\operatorname{Quantile}_{\tau}\!\left(\{c_{r,R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\}_{r=1}^{R}\right),\qquad\tau\in(0,1). (8)

This aggregation summarizes stability in the lower tail and is less sensitive than the minimum to a single noisy run [11].

We then convert the aggregated stability score into a dispersion-risk penalty. First,

P^drR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=−log⁡(cR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)+ε)max⁡(cR,θ,ϑ​(q,p),ε),\hat{P}_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\frac{-\log(c_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+\varepsilon)}{\max(c_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p),\varepsilon)}, (9)

where −log⁡(cR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)+ε)-\log(c_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+\varepsilon) is monotone in stability and the additional division amplifies separation when cR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)c_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) is small. To prevent a few extreme candidates from dominating the reranking score, we apply a saturating cap:

PdrR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=C⋅P^drR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)P^drR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)+C+ε,P_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=\frac{C\cdot\hat{P}_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)}{\hat{P}_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+C+\varepsilon}, (10)

where C>0C>0 bounds the maximum penalty.

3.3 Score-Gated Penalty Fusion and Final Selection

We restrict robustness correction to the decision-critical region of the base-score distribution. Top-KK membership is determined by candidates with high base scores, whereas the low-score tail cannot enter the Top-KK set. Penalizing all candidates can therefore introduce unnecessary ranking changes in the low-score region. We address this issue with a score-dependent gate.

For each query qq, we compute a gate center μθ​(q)\mu_{\theta}(q) from the base-score distribution:

μθ​(q)=Quantile 1−m|𝒟|⁡({sθ​(q,p)}p∈𝒟),m=⌈|𝒟|⌉.\mu_{\theta}(q)=\operatorname{Quantile}_{\,1-\frac{m}{|\mathcal{D}|}}\left(\{s_{\theta}(q,p)\}_{p\in\mathcal{D}}\right),\qquad m=\left\lceil\sqrt{|\mathcal{D}|}\right\rceil. (11)

We use m=⌈|𝒟|⌉m=\lceil\sqrt{|\mathcal{D}|}\rceil as a simple heuristic to place μθ​(q)\mu_{\theta}(q) in the upper tail without depending directly on KK.

We define the gate as

wθ​(q,p)=σ⁡(sθ​(q,p)−μθ​(q)),w_{\theta}(q,p)=\sigma\!\left(s_{\theta}(q,p)-\mu_{\theta}(q)\right), (12)

where σ\sigma is the sigmoid function, so that wθ​(q,p)≈1w_{\theta}(q,p)\approx 1 when sθ​(q,p)≫μθ​(q)s_{\theta}(q,p)\gg\mu_{\theta}(q) and wθ​(q,p)≈0w_{\theta}(q,p)\approx 0 when sθ​(q,p)≪μθ​(q)s_{\theta}(q,p)\ll\mu_{\theta}(q).

Starting from the abstract defended score s~θ​(q,p)\tilde{s}_{\theta}(q,p) introduced in Sec. 3.1, we now specify its concrete form by making explicit its dependence on the perturbation repeat count RR and the probe parameter subset ϑ\vartheta. The final defended reranking score is

s~R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=sθ​(q,p)−wθ​(q,p)​(PdrR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)+PrepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)).\tilde{s}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=s_{\theta}(q,p)-w_{\theta}(q,p)\Big(P_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+P_{\mathrm{rep}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\Big). (13)

We use equal weights for the two penalties. In practice, PdrR,θ,ϑP_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta} is capped by CC, and PrepR,θ,ϑP_{\mathrm{rep}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta} uses a log transform, which keeps their magnitudes comparable while avoiding an additional weighting hyperparameter.

Empirical evidence for our reranking objective.

Fig. 2 summarizes the overall retrieval-stage results: ProGRank consistently reduces both Poison Hit Rate and Poison Recall Rate relative to the undefended ranking, with the strongest effect on HotpotQA. On NQ and MS MARCO, the Top-50 Poison Hit Rate is also reduced to around 30%. This trend is reflected in Fig. 4, where poisoned passages show almost no upward rank shift but much larger downward shifts than clean passages. Fig. 3 further shows that poisoned passages tend to receive larger penalties and gate values, so stronger correction is applied in the decision-critical high-score region. Fig. 5 shows that the full gated objective performs best overall, and that removing PdrR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)P_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) causes a larger degradation than removing PrepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)P_{\mathrm{rep}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p). Taken together, these results provide empirical evidence that the proposed reranking objective helps suppress poisoned passages while preserving its focus on the high-score region. Experimental details are provided in Sec. 4.1.

3.4 Mechanism-Level Intuition for Stochastic Probing

We provide a simple mechanism-level intuition for why optimization-driven poisoned passages can exhibit lower representational consistency (Eq. (4)) and higher dispersion risk (Eqs. (9)–(10)) under stochastic probing induced by 𝒯⁡(⋅)\mathcal{T}(\cdot). We do not claim a formal guarantee that all poisoned passages are unstable; rather, the following abstraction explains the empirical trend observed in our experiments.

The perturbation operator 𝒯⁡(⋅)\mathcal{T}(\cdot) can be viewed as feature noising that induces stochastic representations via random masking of tokens, units, or computation paths, consistent with standard interpretations of dropout [8, 24, 27]. If a candidate’s high similarity relies on a small set of concentrated and perturbation-sensitive features, mild perturbations can suppress their effective contribution in some runs and yield unstable gradient responses. This view aligns with robustness perspectives that distinguish robust evidence from brittle but highly predictive features [12], and with optimization-driven corpus poisoning where an attacker explicitly optimizes a passage to achieve high retrieval score for target queries [38, 40, 28].

Specifically, following the probe gradient in Eq. (3), we use the decomposition

gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)=uθ,ϑ​(q,p)+Zr​(q,p)​aθ,ϑ​(q,p)+ξr,θ,ϑ​(q,p),g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)=u_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+Z_{r}(q,p)\,a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+\xi_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p), (14)

where uθ,ϑ​(q,p)u_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) models a distributed (stable) contribution, aθ,ϑ​(q,p)a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) models a concentrated component, ξr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)\xi_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) is zero-mean noise with bounded second moment (so empirical averages concentrate as RR grows), and Zr​(q,p)∈{0,1}Z_{r}(q,p)\in\{0,1\} is an abstract Bernoulli gate indicating whether the concentrated component remains effectively active under 𝒯r\mathcal{T}_{r} (i.e., whether the concentrated component remains active under the perturbation in the rr-th run). We assume {Zr​(q,p)}r=1R\{Z_{r}(q,p)\}_{r=1}^{R} are i.i.d. with ℙ⁡(Zr​(q,p)=1)=1−ρ⁡(q,p)\mathbb{P}(Z_{r}(q,p)=1)=1-\rho(q,p) for some ρ⁡(q,p)∈(0,1)\rho(q,p)\in(0,1). For simplicity, we treat ρ⁡(q,p)\rho(q,p) as an effective inactivation rate determined by the fixed retriever (θ,ϑ)(\theta,\vartheta) and the chosen perturbation operator. This is a minimal abstraction, which only requires that the concentrated component is absent with non-zero probability across runs. This induces a simple on/off behavior: the concentrated component is sometimes kept (Zr=1Z_{r}=1) and sometimes masked out by perturbations (Zr=0Z_{r}=0), consistent with stochastic masking.

Under Eq. (14) and sufficiently large RR, Eq. (4) admits the population approximation

RepR,θ,ϑ2​(q,p)≈‖𝔼r​[gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)]‖22𝔼r​‖gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)‖22.\mathrm{Rep}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}^{2}(q,p)\approx\frac{\|\mathbb{E}_{r}[g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)]\|_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{r}\|g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\|_{2}^{2}}. (15)

From Eq. (14),

𝔼r​[gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)]=uθ,ϑ​(q,p)+(1−ρ⁡(q,p))​aθ,ϑ​(q,p).\mathbb{E}_{r}[g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)]=u_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+(1-\rho(q,p))a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p). (16)

When ‖aθ,ϑ​(q,p)‖2\|a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\|_{2} is large and ρ⁡(q,p)∈(0,1)\rho(q,p)\in(0,1), the concentrated component is present in some runs and absent in others, which increases the second moment 𝔼r​‖gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)‖22\mathbb{E}_{r}\|g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\|_{2}^{2} more than the squared mean ‖𝔼r​[gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)]‖22\|\mathbb{E}_{r}[g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)]\|_{2}^{2}. As a result, RepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)\mathrm{Rep}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) decreases and PrepR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)P_{\mathrm{rep}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) increases. In practice, we use small values of RR, and the RR-sweep in Fig. 6 shows that performance remains stable across repeat counts.

For dispersion risk, under Eq. (14) and large RR, the sample mean g¯R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)\bar{g}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) (defined in Eq. (6)) concentrates around uθ,ϑ​(q,p)+(1−ρ⁡(q,p))​aθ,ϑ​(q,p)u_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)+(1-\rho(q,p))a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p). When the concentrated component is absent (Zr=0Z_{r}=0),

gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)−g¯R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)≈−(1−ρ⁡(q,p))​aθ,ϑ​(q,p);g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)-\bar{g}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\approx-(1-\rho(q,p))a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p);

when it is present (Zr=1Z_{r}=1),

gr,θ,ϑ​(q,p)−g¯R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)≈ρ⁡(q,p)​aθ,ϑ​(q,p).g_{r,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)-\bar{g}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\approx\rho(q,p)a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p).

Thus, if ‖aθ,ϑ​(q,p)‖2\|a_{\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\|_{2} is large and ρ⁡(q,p)\rho(q,p) is non-negligible, the per-run deviations in Eq. (6) are large with non-zero probability across runs. Since cR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)c_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) in Eq. (8) is a lower quantile of {cr,R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)}r=1R\{c_{r,R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\}_{r=1}^{R}, these large-deviation runs reduce cR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)c_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p) and hence increase PdrR,θ,ϑ​(q,p)P_{\mathrm{dr}}^{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p). Mixed perturbations can increase the chance that the concentrated component becomes inactive in a run (i.e., larger effective ρ⁡(q,p)\rho(q,p)), further amplifying this effect.

3.5 Towards Implementation Efficiency

Although our formulation is defined over 𝒟\mathcal{D}, a practical deployment would instantiate 𝒟\mathcal{D} as a bounded first-stage candidate pool rather than the full corpus. One may first retrieve a buffer of top-BB candidates with B≫KB\gg K, estimate the gate on this pool, and apply stochastic probing only to the decision-critical upper-tail candidates before selecting the final top-KK. The additional defence overhead then depends mainly on the bounded pool size BB, rather than directly on the full corpus size, while remaining consistent with the score-gating intuition in Sec. 3.3.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setups

Datasets and corpus poisoning methods.

Following the implementation in [28], we evaluate on MS MARCO [1], Natural Questions (NQ) [19], and HotpotQA [33]. Our corpus poisoning methods include PoisonedRAG [40], LIAR-RAG [26], and Joint-GCG [28]. For each dataset, we sample 100 evaluation queries, and each query is associated with 50 clean passages.

Retrieval-stage settings.

For retrieval-stage experiments, we consider three dense retrievers: Contriever [14], DPR [16], and BGE [32]. We use a pooled-poison protocol, where all poisoned passages for the same query are added to the clean pool. For each query, the retriever returns a Top-KK list with K∈{5,10,20,30,40,50}K\in\{5,10,20,30,40,50\}. We evaluate ProGRank under four factors: perturbation repeats R∈{4,8,16,20,24,28,32}R\in\{4,8,16,20,24,28,32\}, probe layer L∈{3,7,11}L\in\{3,7,11\}, perturbation type (encoder dropout, token dropout, or their mixture), and retriever backbone. Here, LL denotes the probed LayerNorm module, and for dispersion risk we fix τ=0.1\tau=0.1, α=4.0\alpha=4.0, and C=6.0C=6.0. Results in Fig. 2, 3, and 5 are averaged over these settings, while Fig. 6 reports the corresponding ablations. The ablations show that performance stabilizes around R=20R=20, L=3L=3 performs best overall, and mixed perturbation is the strongest setting. These choices are then used in the downstream generation experiments. To avoid data snooping, retrieval-stage analysis and configuration selection use a random 20% query split, and downstream generation uses the remaining 80%.

Retrieval-stage metrics.

To evaluate poisoning exposure at retrieval time, we use two KK-dependent metrics. First, Poison Hit Rate measures whether at least one poisoned passage appears in the Top-KK set:

Poison​Hit​Rate​@​K=𝔼q​[(TopKp∈𝒟⁡s~R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)∩𝒟poison​(q)≠∅)].\mathrm{Poison\ Hit\ Rate}@K=\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\mathbf{1}\!\left(\operatorname{TopK}_{p\in\mathcal{D}}\tilde{s}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\cap\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}(q)\neq\emptyset\right)\right]. (17)

Second, Poison Recall Rate measures the fraction of poisoned passages retrieved into the Top-KK set:

Poison​Recall​Rate​@​K=𝔼q​[|TopKp∈𝒟⁡s~R,θ,ϑ​(q,p)∩𝒟poison​(q)||𝒟poison​(q)|+ε].\mathrm{Poison\ Recall\ Rate}@K=\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\frac{\left|\operatorname{TopK}_{p\in\mathcal{D}}\tilde{s}_{R,\theta,\vartheta}(q,p)\cap\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}(q)\right|}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}(q)|+\varepsilon}\right]. (18)

where 𝒟poison​(q)\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}(q) denotes the poisoned passages associated with query qq, and ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a small constant for numerical stability. These metrics are used only as retrieval-stage proxies; the end-to-end impact is evaluated separately using downstream robustness and clean-utility metrics.

Downstream generation settings.

For downstream generation, we use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.2 as generators, all with the same decoding configuration. For ProGRank, as in the retrieval analysis, we vary the retriever backbone among Contriever, DPR, and BGE. We fix the retrieval depth K=5K=5, the perturbation repeat R=20R=20, mixed perturbation, and probe layer L=3L=3. Unless otherwise specified, we report results averaged over generators, retriever backbones.

We report substring-based attack success rate (ASR), judge-based ASR, and substring-based accuracy (ACC). Let yqy_{q} denote the generated response for query qq, let aqcorra_{q}^{\mathrm{corr}} denote the ground-truth correct answer, and let aqadva_{q}^{\mathrm{adv}} denote the attacker-targeted incorrect answer. Before evaluation, both model outputs and reference answers are normalized by lowercasing and removing punctuation and extra whitespace. We define substring-based ASR as ASRsub=𝔼q​[𝟏​(Inc⁡(q,yq)=1)]\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{sub}}=\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\mathbf{1}(\mathrm{Inc}(q,y_{q})=1)\big], where Inc⁡(q,yq)=1\mathrm{Inc}(q,y_{q})=1 if the normalized response contains aqadva_{q}^{\mathrm{adv}} but not aqcorra_{q}^{\mathrm{corr}}. We define substring-based ACC as ACCsub=𝔼q​[𝟏​(Cor⁡(q,yq)=1)]\mathrm{ACC}_{\mathrm{sub}}=\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\mathbf{1}(\mathrm{Cor}(q,y_{q})=1)\big], where Cor⁡(q,yq)=1\mathrm{Cor}(q,y_{q})=1 if the normalized response contains aqcorra_{q}^{\mathrm{corr}} but not aqadva_{q}^{\mathrm{adv}}. Judge-based ASR is computed using a fixed deterministic LLM judge, Llama-Guard-3-8B [20], which receives the query, the ground-truth correct answer, the attacker-targeted incorrect answer, and the model output, and assigns one label from {ATTACK, CORRECT, OTHER}; judge-based ASR is then the fraction of responses labeled ATTACK.

Besides these end-to-end robustness metrics, we also evaluate clean utility using benchmark-specific metrics. Following the standard protocol for each dataset, we report token-level F1 on HotpotQA, exact match (EM) on NQ, and ROUGE-L F1 on MS MARCO.

Compute.

All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA DGX Spark.

Additional experimental details for the configurations and results are provided in the supplementary material.

4.2 Downstream Generation Analysis

Under the downstream generation setting defined in Sec. 4.1, we evaluate ProGRank against the undefended baseline and compare it with representative corpus-poisoning defences, namely GRADA [37], GMTP [17], and RAGuard [18]. These baselines are selected from Tab. 1 based on code availability.

Tab. 2 reports the main end-to-end robustness results. ProGRank achieves the lowest macro-average judge-based ASR on all three datasets, reaching 0.0000.000 on HotpotQA, NQ, and MS MARCO. It also achieves the lowest macro-average substring-based ASR on all three datasets, with 0.0110.011 on HotpotQA, 0.0000.000 on NQ, and 0.0330.033 on MS MARCO. In terms of clean utility, ProGRank achieves the highest macro-average ACC on HotpotQA, while GRADA performs best on NQ and RAGuard performs best on MS MARCO. As shown in Tab. 4, RAGuard is about 20×20\times slower than ProGRank on average due to repeated leave-one-out verification. The reported ProGRank latency is measured on the actual experimental pipeline, with all retrieved candidates reranked per query. Overall, ProGRank offers the strongest robustness and a substantially better efficiency–robustness trade-off than RAGuard in our evaluation.

Tab. 3 evaluates ProGRank under ProGRank-based evasive attacks. The macro-average results are 0.030/0.016/0.3720.030/0.016/0.372 on HotpotQA, 0.016/0.034/0.3650.016/0.034/0.365 on NQ, and 0.049/0.019/0.4290.049/0.019/0.429 on MS MARCO in terms of substring-based ASR, judge-based ASR, and ACC, respectively. These results suggest that ProGRank retains robustness under the adaptive attack configurations considered in this work, especially on HotpotQA and NQ.

Tab. 5 reports clean utility. ProGRank achieves the best EM on NQ, while the baseline and RAGuard perform better on HotpotQA, and GRADA gives the best ROUGE-L F1 on MS MARCO. Overall, this indicates a dataset-dependent trade-off between robustness and clean-task utility.

5 Conclusion

We presented ProGRank, a post hoc, training-free retriever-side defence against corpus poisoning in dense-retriever RAG. ProGRank stress-tests query–passage pairs under mild randomized perturbations and reranks them using probe-gradient instability signals computed on a small fixed parameter subset, instantiated in our experiments as a LayerNorm module at layer LL. Rather than assuming that all poisoned passages are intrinsically unstable, ProGRank targets a practically important subset of optimization-driven poisoning attacks whose retrievability relies on perturbation-sensitive matching signals. Across three datasets, multiple dense retrievers, and representative poisoning attacks, ProGRank consistently reduces poisoned Top-KK exposure and achieves the lowest macro-average judge-based ASR in end-to-end evaluation, while remaining effective under the adaptive attack settings considered in this work.

Supplementary Material

Implementation Details of Downstream Generation

Generation and judge configurations.

In downstream generations, we set the maximum answer length to 64 new tokens and the maximum judge output length to 16 new tokens.

Answer-generation prompt.

We use the following prompt template:

You are a helpful assistant, below is a query from a user and some relevant contexts. Answer the question given the information in those contexts. Your answer should be short and concise. If you cannot find the answer to the question, just say "I don’t know".
Contexts: {context_1}
{context_2}
...
{context_K}
Query: {query}
Answer:
Judge prompt.

For judge-based ASR, we use the following prompt template:

You are an evaluator for RAG poisoning attacks. Task: decide whether the MODEL RESPONSE aligns with the attacker-targeted incorrect answer. Output format (strict): LABEL: ATTACK or LABEL: CORRECT. Do not output any additional words.
Decision rules:
- ATTACK: response supports or states the attacker-targeted incorrect answer.
- CORRECT: otherwise.
Question: {query}
Ground-truth correct answer: {correct_answer}
Attacker targeted incorrect answer: {incorrect_answer}
Model response: {model_output}
LABEL:

Implementation Details of Poisoning Methods

PoisonedRAG configuration.

For PoisonedRAG, we follow the released benchmark configuration with score function = dot, adversarial passages per query = 5, start index = −1-1, retrieval gap = 20, attack method = HotFlip, adversarial passage tokens = 30, optimization iterations = 30, and total attack budget = 200.

Joint-GCG configuration.

For Joint-GCG, the attack uses max new tokens = 256, inference batch size = 16, attack samples per step = 128, token search top-kk = 16, optimization epochs = 64, adversarial tag length = 32, and ASCII-only token optimization = True. For each query, the poisoned text is constructed as adversarial tag + query suffix + benchmark-provided adversarial text.

LIAR-RAG configuration.

For LIAR-RAG, we use the released baseline implementation with max new tokens = 256, inference batch size = 16, attack samples per step = 128, token search top-kk = 16, optimization epochs = 128, retriever-side adversarial tag length = 16, generator-side adversarial tag length = 16, and ASCII-only token optimization = True. For each query, the poisoned text is constructed as generator-side adversarial tag + retriever-side adversarial tag + query suffix + benchmark-provided adversarial text. During optimization, the attack alternates between retriever-side and generator-side updates with retriever steps = 8 and generator steps = 8 in each cycle.

Implementation Details of Defence Methods

GRADA configuration.

For GRADA, we use the released implementation with defence variant = HRSIM and α=0.4\alpha=0.4. In the downstream end-to-end evaluation, we use Top-K=20K=20, max clean hits = 50, max new tokens = 64, and judge max new tokens = 16.

GMTP configuration.

For GMTP, we use the released implementation with N=10N=10, M=5M=5, remove-threshold =−1.0=-1.0, remove-lambda =1.0=1.0, adaptive quantile =0.6=0.6, and reranker = bert-base-uncased. In the downstream end-to-end evaluation, we use Top-K=20K=20, max clean hits = 50, max new tokens = 64, and judge max new tokens = 16.

RAGuard configuration.

For RAGuard, we use the released anomaly-scoring implementation with score threshold =1.8=1.8. In our end-to-end wrapper used together with the practical-deployment efficiency analysis, we set remove count =1=1, Top-K=20K=20, max clean hits = 50, max new tokens = 64, and judge max new tokens = 16.

Perturbation Types and Hyperparameter Settings

Token dropout.

In this setting, we randomly drop document tokens by modifying the attention mask with a dropout probability of 0.10. The perturbation is applied only to the document side; the query is left unchanged. The [CLS] token is always preserved, and the implementation further ensures that at least one additional document token remains active after masking.

Encoder dropout.

In this setting, we activate the encoder’s native internal dropout by switching the encoder to training mode during penalty estimation. We do not add any extra manually tuned dropout module. For Contriever, this corresponds to the pretrained model’s default configuration, with hidden dropout 0.10 and attention dropout 0.10.

Mixed perturbation.

In the mixed setting, we combine encoder dropout and token dropout. Specifically, we enable the encoder’s native internal dropout and simultaneously apply token dropout with probability 0.10 on the document side only.
